content: Parke-Davis, now a subsidiary of Pfizer, was once the oldest and largest pharmaceutical company in the United States. It played a significant role in medical history, having been founded in Detroit, Michigan, in 1886 by Hervey Parke and George Davis. At its peak, it was the largest pharmaceutical company in the world and is credited with establishing the first modern pharmaceutical laboratory and developing the first systematic methods for conducting clinical trials of new medications. In 1970, Parke-Davis was acquired by Warner-Lambert, which was later purchased by Pfizer in 2000. One of Parke-Davis' early products was an amylase enzyme isolated from Aspergillus oryzae by Dr. Jokichi Takamine. Initially intended for use in distilleries, the enzyme was more successfully marketed as Taka-diastase for the treatment of dyspepsia. In 1962, the company developed Ketalar (ketamine hydrochloride), an anesthetic for horses and a dissociative drug. Dr. Takamine also developed a pure form of adrenaline, which was patented in 1900 and trademarked as Adrenalin. Due to the similarity of this name to adrenaline, the alternative name epinephrine was mandated for generic use in the United States, a practice that continues today. The patent for adrenaline was challenged by K. Mulford on the grounds that it was a natural product and therefore not patentable. However, Judge Learned Hand ruled in favor of Parke-Davis, a decision that remains a cornerstone of modern patent law. Before cocaine was criminalized, Parke-Davis sold it in various forms, including cigarettes, powder, and injectable mixtures. The company also patented phencyclidine (PCP) in the 1950s, a drug now classified as a Schedule II substance under the Convention on Psychotropic Substances. Parke-Davis introduced Dilantin, the first widely available treatment for epilepsy, in 1939, although the company neither discovered the compound nor its application. It also developed the first bacterial vaccine and was recognized as a pioneer in vaccinology. Parke-Davis was one of five companies contracted to manufacture the Salk polio vaccine, which helped eradicate polio. In 1954, the company developed Quadrigen, a combination of the DPT and polio vaccines, which was approved in 1959 but later withdrawn in 1968 due to lawsuits over adverse effects in vaccinated children. Other notable products included anti-infectives and combined oral contraceptive pills. In modern times, Parke-Davis faced legal challenges. In the 2002 case of Franklin v. Parke-Davis, the company was accused of illegal marketing practices, including promoting off-label uses of its anticonvulsant medication Neurontin. Approximately $8 billion in sales were attributed to indications not approved by the FDA. In 2004, Pfizer admitted to aggressively marketing Neurontin for unapproved conditions such as bipolar disorder, pain, migraines, and drug and alcohol withdrawal. Pfizer agreed to pay $430 million in penalties, although it claimed the violations occurred before its acquisition of Warner-Lambert in 2000. On January 22, 2007, Pfizer announced the closure of its research facilities in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Actor Calvert DeForest, known for his appearances with David Letterman, worked for Parke-Davis for many years.
